chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hashim, from Sufyan al-Jariri, from Abu Maryam al-Ansari, from Harun ibn Antara, from his father who said:

I heard the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) again and again, and he was saying with his fingers clasped one into the other: 'My ease is my constraint, and my constraint is my ease.' Then he said: 'Destroyed are the expectants (who expect it now), and rescued are the steadfast (who expect it soon). The pebbles are fixed upon their pegs. I swear by Allah a true oath that after the grief is a wonderful victory.'

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful (Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.الْمَحَاضِيرُ: The expectants (those who wait for the reappearance, often interpreted as those who wait passively or with anxiety)
key_terms.الْمُقَرَّبُونَ: The steadfast/confirmed (those who are close to God and steadfast in waiting)

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'My ease is my constraint' in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights Imam Ali’s (AS) profound insight into the dialectic of hardship and relief, using the physical gesture of clasping fingers to symbolize the tightening and loosening of divine decree. It distinguishes between the *Mahadir*—those who remain passive or anxious in waiting—and the *Muqarrabun*, the spiritually confirmed who actively endure trials, promising them ultimate salvation. This reflects the Shia theological emphasis on *Sabr* (steadfastness) as an active, transformative state rather than mere endurance.
